crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Credit Scoring with Alternative Data
children.blurb: Credit scoring with alternative data covers the use of nontraditional records, such as rent, utility, telecom, cash flow, and public records, to estimate repayment risk when traditional bureau files are thin or stale.

children.name: Covenant Extraction
children.blurb: Covenant extraction is the work of turning the terms of credit agreements, indentures, and loan documents into structured data that a credit team can query and monitor.

children.name: Predicting Distress and Default
children.blurb: Predicting distress and default covers the estimation of a borrower's or issuer's likelihood of failing to meet debt obligations over horizons set by the portfolio or regulatory context.

children.name: Modelling the Yield Curve
children.blurb: Modelling the yield curve covers the estimation of the term structure of interest rates from market prices, including spot rates, forward rates, discount factors and par yields.

children.name: Stress Testing Structured Credit
children.blurb: Stress testing structured credit covers securitized products such as RMBS, CMBS, ABS, CLOs and CDOs, and the tranches that sit on top of underlying pools.

sections.body: Fixed income and credit risk is the part of finance that asks whether a borrower will pay back what they owe, and what a lender should charge for that risk. Artificial intelligence is now used across this work in concrete ways: models score loan applicants using bank records, phone data and payment histories, language models read loan agreements to pull out the covenants that restrict a borrower, and classifiers flag companies whose financial signals resemble those of past defaults. Traders and risk desks also use machine learning to fit the yield curve from bond prices and to run stress scenarios on pools of mortgages and other structured debt. The work is mostly statistical pattern finding on large datasets, not reasoning about the economy, and every model inherits the biases and gaps of the data it was trained on.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Credit scoring is the most mature area, with machine learning in wide production use, though regulators in several jurisdictions require lenders to explain decisions, which limits how opaque a model can be. Covenant extraction has improved sharply with language models but still needs human review, because a missed or misread clause can misprice a loan. Distress prediction works better at ranking relative risk than at calling the timing of a specific default, and it degrades when the economy shifts away from the conditions in the training data. Yield curve modelling is largely a curve fitting and forecasting problem where machine learning competes with, rather than replaces, established term structure models. Stress testing structured credit remains the weakest link, because the tail scenarios that matter most are rare, and historical data on them is thin.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The five pages here follow the chain from a single borrower to a whole portfolio. Credit Scoring with Alternative Data covers who gets a loan and at what price, and is the place to start for the consumer side. Covenant Extraction deals with the contract language that governs a loan once it exists, and matters most to anyone reading the terms rather than the score. Predicting Distress and Default moves from the individual borrower to the question of whether a firm or issuer will fail, which feeds directly into bond pricing. Modelling the Yield Curve supplies the discounting and rate backdrop that every other page depends on. Stress Testing Structured Credit sits at the end of the chain, taking the scores, covenants, default signals and rates and asking what happens to a pool of debt under a severe shock.
